title: Taming Generative Co-Folding Prior for Molecular Docking with Diffusion Bridge
claim: Prior approaches predict directly or generate from pure noise; ours starts from a structural prior and bridges it to the target.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dashed dividers, parallel input→module→output flows
description: Three side-by-side panels separated by dashed gray vertical lines, each showing a top-to-bottom flow with black arrows. Left: Protein and Ligand structure renders feed into a pale purple 'Docking Model' box, which outputs a Holo Complex image. Middle: a Noise cloud on top, plus Sequence (colored amino-acid tokens A G L Y K) and SMILES (molecule document icon) entering from the left, feed a blue 'Diffusion module' box that yields a Holo Complex. Right: the same layout, but the top input is an Apo protein structure and the module is a green 'Diffusion Bridge' box, again producing a Holo Complex. The eye goes first to the colored module boxes. The changed input (Noise replaced by Apo) and the changed module color mark the difference.
caption: Comparison of three paradigms for protein-ligand docking. Left: Traditional deep learning-based methods directly predict holo complexes from protein and ligand inputs. Middle: Recent co-folding methods formulate docking as a generation process starting from noise. Right: BridgeDock leverages apo structures as explicit structural priors and formulates docking as an apo-to-holo diffusion bridge.
abstract: Molecular docking aims to predict the three-dimensional structure of a protein-ligand complex; in the conventional structure-based setting, it is conditioned on an input protein structure and ligand, often starting from an apo receptor in flexible docking or a holo receptor in rigid docking. Recent co-folding models exemplified by AlphaFold 3 achieve strong accuracy in protein-ligand complex prediction, but they typically generate complexes from sequence-derived inputs and therefore do not directly use apo structures as structural priors in docking, leading to a larger conformational search space and weaker robustness in difficult or few-step settings. We present BridgeDock, a framework that adapts pretrained co-folding backbones to flexible docking by modeling the apo-to-holo transition as a diffusion bridge, allowing generation from the initial protein-ligand state rather than from Gaussian noise. To make this bridge formulation compatible with pretrained denoisers, we introduce an alignment mechanism that maps bridge states to the original denoising schedule of the pretrained model. Experiments on standard flexible docking benchmarks show that BridgeDock consistently outperforms strong co-folding baselines. Moreover, BridgeDock is computationally efficient at inference time and remains effective even with very few denoising steps.
